item.content:encoded:
Sanctions in the Diplomatic Equation

发布源: 47. Russian International Affairs Council (RIAC) --Russia | 抓取时间: 2026-09-29

Login if you are already registered

Doctor of Political Science, Director General of the Russian International Affairs Council, RIAC member

Short versionof the article

Full versionof the article

The latest round of Russian–American talks has drawn attention to the sanctions dimension. It was reported that Gene Lange—the Acting Under Secretary of the US Treasury—took part in them. He is a fairly significant figure in his own right. Besides financial sanctions, his portfolio also covers financial intelligence and counter–terrorism financing. Of course, he is not the only one overseeing sanctions within the Administration. Some of these powers are concentrated in the State Department. The Department of Commerce also plays a huge role, since export controls fall within its remit. Yet financial restrictions can be regarded as the most significant of all, and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which sits within the US Treasury, has long since become the bureaucratic “brand” of American sanctions.

Sanctions are a foreign–policy instrument. They are used in diplomatic bargaining. This means the American side itself has an interest in their flexibility—that is, in the ability to reduce their intensity even where they have been enshrined in law.
